title: "Fitting ecological response curves"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
# Load ggplot2 for the consistently formatted rendered figures in this chapter.
library(ggplot2)
```

# Introduction

In this chapter, we learn how to fit an ecological response curve to data: a deterministic
function of a predictor describes one parameter of the distribution of each observation
(usually its mean), and the parameters of the function are estimated by maximum likelihood.
Once the curve is fitted, we estimate the uncertainty of its parameters and of the curve
itself, check whether the fitted model describes the data, revise the model where it does
not, and compare it with alternative models.

The chapter brings together the two pillars of the book, probability distributions and
likelihood ([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd) to [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd))
and deterministic functions ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd)). What is new is the
likelihood of a response curve, in which every observation has a distribution of its own;
how RTMB calculates the gradient of the negative log-likelihood that the optimiser uses;
the uncertainty of a fitted curve; residuals calculated by simulation from the fitted
model; and a further information criterion for comparing models, the Bayesian information
criterion (BIC). One example runs through the chapter, the functional response of
dragonfly larvae that prey on reed frog tadpoles (Vonesh and Bolker 2005).^[Vonesh, J. R.
and Bolker, B. M. (2005), "Compensatory larval responses shift trade-offs associated with
predator-induced hatching plasticity", *Ecology* 86: 1580–1591. The data are in the
package `emdbook`.] These are the data that Chapter 5 used as a backdrop and for which it
read starting values by eye. The observations are numbers of tadpoles killed out of a known
number, so the distributions of the chapter are the Binomial and the Beta-Binomial, and the
residuals are calculated with the package DHARMa. Every tank is treated as an independent
observation; [Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) extends the models to observations that
come in groups.

# Learning goals

In this chapter, we will cover:

- a response curve as a parameter of a distribution;
- the likelihood of a response curve and its fit;
- how RTMB calculates the gradient of the negative log-likelihood;
- standard errors, correlation and likelihood profile intervals of the parameters of a
  curve;
- the uncertainty of the fitted curve;
- simulation from a fitted model and scaled quantile residuals;
- a model for overdispersed proportions;
- model comparison with AIC, AICc and BIC.

We will use the [Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-binomial) and
[Beta-Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-beta_binomial) entries of the
distribution supplement and the
[Michaelis–Menten](../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) entry
of the function supplement.

The table below is a roadmap of the chapter. Each row is one step, with the question that
it answers and the R tools that we use for it.

| Step | Question it answers | In R |
|---|---|---|
| The model | Which parameter of which distribution does the curve describe? | `plogis()`, `exp()` |
| The fit | Which parameter values make the observed counts most probable? | NLL with the predictor in the list of data, `MakeADFun()`, `optim()` |
| The gradient | How does the optimiser know in which direction to move? | `obj$gr()` |
| Uncertainty of the parameters | How precisely are the parameters of the curve estimated? | `sdreport()`, `cov2cor()`, `TMB::tmbprofile()`, `confint()` |
| Uncertainty of the curve | How precisely is the curve itself estimated? | `ADREPORT()` on a grid of the predictor |
| Checking the model | Does the fitted model describe the data? | `OBS()`, `obj$simulate()`, `DHARMa::createDHARMa()` |
| Revising the observation model | What if the counts vary more than the model allows? | `dbetabinom()` |
| Comparison | Which of the candidate models do the data support? | AIC, AICc and BIC from `fit$value` |

: Roadmap of the chapter.

# From a response curve to a model for observations {#sec-response-observation}

A **response curve** gives one parameter of the distribution of each observation as a
function of a predictor. Let $Y_i$ be the $i$-th observation and $x_i$ the value of the
predictor at which it was made. The parameter $\theta_i$ of its distribution is

$$
\theta_i=f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta),
$$

where $f$ is a deterministic function of the kind studied in
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd) and $\boldsymbol\beta$ is the vector of its parameters
(the semicolon separates the input of the function from its parameters). Usually
$\theta_i$ is the mean, because the curves of Chapter 5 describe how an expected response
changes with a predictor. The other parameters of the distribution, such as the standard
deviation of a Normal model or the shape of a Negative Binomial model, are often shared by
all the observations. So every observation has a distribution of the same family, but with
its own value of the parameter that follows the curve.

The curve must return a value in the range of the parameter that it describes. A mean
count cannot be negative and a probability must lie between 0 and 1, whereas the functions
of Chapter 5 are not restricted in this way for every value of their parameters and of
$x$. The table gives the usual cases.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-composition) showed how to give a curve
the range that a quantity requires, by passing it through an outer function.

| Distribution | Parameter that follows the curve | Range | How to give the curve that range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | mean $\mu$ | any real value | any curve |
| Poisson, Negative Binomial | mean $\mu$ | positive | a curve that is positive for every $x$, or the exponential of another curve |
| Binomial | probability $p$ | between 0 and 1 | a curve between 0 and 1 for every $x$, or the inverse logit of another curve |

: Parameters that a response curve describes, and how a curve is given their range.

As in [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd), we treat the observations as independent. They
are no longer identically distributed, however: two observations made at different values
of the predictor have different distributions, and the distribution of each observation
depends on the known value of its predictor. This is the change from Chapter 4, where every
observation had the same distribution. Note also that the observation model is a choice, in
the same way as the curve is (see "Choosing a distribution" in
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-discrete_distributions)), and in this chapter we
will revise it.

Let's write the model for the reed frog experiment. Sixteen tanks were stocked with
$N_i$ tadpoles, from 5 to 100, together with three dragonfly larvae, and $K_i$ is the number
of tadpoles killed in tank $i$ in 14 days. Each tadpole of a tank is either killed or not,
so we use a [Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-binomial) model with $N_i$
trials, in which the curve gives the probability that a tadpole is killed:

$$
K_i \sim \operatorname{Binomial}\left(N_i,\,p(N_i)\right),
\qquad
p(N)=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha HN},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,16,
$$

where $\alpha$ is the attack rate and $H$ the handling time of the Holling type II form of
the disc equation ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation)). Here the
predictor, the initial number of tadpoles, is also the number of trials. The curve
describes the probability and not the number killed, because a Binomial distribution is
written in terms of the number of trials and a probability. The expected number killed is
then

$$
E[K_i]=N_i\,p(N_i)=\frac{\alpha N_i}{1+\alpha HN_i},
$$

the disc equation of Chapter 5. Under the assumptions of the disc equation, the probability
of being killed decreases with density because the larvae spend more of their time handling
the prey that they have caught. The
units follow from Chapter 5: the tadpoles killed were counted over the whole experiment,
so $\alpha$ is a fraction per experiment (at low density, a tadpole is killed with
probability close to $\alpha$) and $H$ is in experiments per tadpole killed. With
$0<\alpha<1$ and $H>0$, the probability $p(N)$ lies between 0 and $\alpha$ for every density,
so this curve has the range that the Binomial distribution requires without an outer
function; when we fit it, we keep $\alpha$ between 0 and 1 and $H$ positive with the
transformations of Chapter 4. We treat the 16 tanks as independent. The Binomial model also
assumes that, within a tank, every tadpole has the same probability of being killed,
independently of the others, which we check in @sec-response-residuals.

@fig-curve_distribution shows what the model says about the data, with the parameter values
that Chapter 5 read by eye ($\alpha=0.5$ per experiment and $H=1/60$ experiments per tadpole
killed). The curve gives the expected number killed at every density, and around it, at
each density, the Binomial distribution gives the probability of every possible number
killed. The spread of that distribution increases with the number of tadpoles in the tank.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curve_distribution
#| fig-cap: "Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points) against the initial number of tadpoles per tank. The line is the expected number killed under the Holling type II curve with the values read by eye in Chapter 5 (α = 0.5 per experiment, H = 1/60 experiments per tadpole killed). The horizontal bars show the Binomial probability of each number killed in a tank with 10, 50 and 100 tadpoles; their length is proportional to the probability."
# Reed frog functional response.
data(ReedfrogFuncresp, package = "emdbook")

# Expected number killed with the values read by eye in Chapter 5.
alpha_eye = 0.5
H_eye = 1 / 60
curve_eye = data.frame(initial = seq(from = 0, to = 100, length.out = 200))
curve_eye$killed = curve_eye$initial * alpha_eye /
  (1 + alpha_eye * H_eye * curve_eye$initial)

# Binomial probabilities at three densities, drawn as horizontal bars that start at the
# density. Probabilities below 0.002 are left out.
bar_scale = 40
mass_data = NULL
for (n_tadpoles in c(10, 50, 100)) {
  killed_values = 0:n_tadpoles
  p_eye = alpha_eye / (1 + alpha_eye * H_eye * n_tadpoles)
  probability = dbinom(x = killed_values, size = n_tadpoles, prob = p_eye)
  keep = probability > 0.002
  mass_data = rbind(
    mass_data,
    data.frame(
      initial = n_tadpoles,
      killed = killed_values[keep],
      probability = probability[keep]
    )
  )
}

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = mass_data,
    aes(
      x = initial, xend = initial + bar_scale * probability,
      y = killed, yend = killed
    ),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = curve_eye,
    aes(x = initial, y = killed),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ReedfrogFuncresp,
    aes(x = Initial, y = Killed),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(x = "Initial number of tadpoles per tank", y = "Tadpoles killed in 14 days") +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {#imp-seedlings-light .callout-important title="seedlings and light"}

The number of tree seedlings in a quadrat is described with a Poisson distribution whose
parameter follows a curve of the light that reaches the soil, $x$ (% of full sunlight).
Which parameter of the distribution does the curve describe, and which values must it
return? Could the straight line $a+bx$ be used for every value of $a$ and $b$? Could the
Michaelis–Menten function $ax/(b+x)$ with positive $a$ and $b$, if some quadrats have no
light at all?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The curve describes the mean $\lambda$ of the Poisson distribution, the expected number of
seedlings per quadrat, which must be positive. The straight line becomes negative for some
values of $x$ unless $a$ and $b$ are restricted, so it cannot be used for every value of
its parameters. The
Michaelis–Menten function is positive for $x>0$, but it is zero at $x=0$. A Poisson
distribution with a mean of zero gives probability one to a count of zero, so a quadrat
without light that contains a seedling would have a probability of zero under the model,
and the log-likelihood could not be calculated.

:::
::::

# Fitting a response curve by maximum likelihood {#sec-fit-response}

The likelihood of a response curve is calculated as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood): the observations are independent, so
the log-likelihood is the sum of the log probabilities (or densities) of the observations.
The difference is that each probability is calculated with the parameter of its own
distribution, which the curve gives at the predictor value of that observation:

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(P(Y_i=y_i\mid\boldsymbol\beta)\right),
$$

where $y_i$ is the observed value of $Y_i$ and $P(Y_i=y_i\mid\boldsymbol\beta)$ is the
probability that the model assigns to it when the parameter of its distribution is
$f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta)$ (any shared parameter of the distribution is added to
$\boldsymbol\beta$). Everything else is the same as in Chapter 4: we write the negative
log-likelihood (NLL) with two lists, transform the constrained parameters, connect the NLL
to the data with `cmb()`, process it with `MakeADFun()`, minimise it with `optim()` and
check the convergence. Two things are new. The list of data holds the predictor as well as
the response, and the starting values of the parameters of the curve are read from a plot
of the data, as in "Starting values by eye" in
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-starting-values).

For the reed frog tanks the log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\alpha,H)=\sum_{i=1}^{16}\log\left(\binom{N_i}{K_i}\,p(N_i)^{K_i}
\left(1-p(N_i)\right)^{N_i-K_i}\right),
\qquad
p(N_i)=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha HN_i}.
$$

We load RTMB and RTMBdist and the data of the experiment, and put the two variables that
the NLL uses in the list of data: `initial`, the number of tadpoles at the start of the
experiment in each tank (the predictor and the number of trials), and `killed`, the number
killed (the response):

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Reed frog functional response (see ?emdbook::ReedfrogFuncresp): the initial number of
# tadpoles (Initial) and the number killed in 14 days (Killed) in each of 16 tanks.
data(ReedfrogFuncresp, package = "emdbook")
frog_data = list(initial = ReedfrogFuncresp$Initial, killed = ReedfrogFuncresp$Killed)
```

The NLL transforms the parameters, calculates the curve and adds up the log probabilities.
The attack rate is a probability, so the optimiser works with its logit, `logit_alpha`,
which `plogis()` turns back into $\alpha$; the handling time is positive, so the optimiser
works with its logarithm, `log_H`. Because `initial` is a vector, the line of the curve
returns a vector with one probability for each tank, and `dbinom()` uses the number of
trials and the probability of each tank:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  # Probability that a tadpole is killed, at the density of each tank.
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
```

Chapter 5 read $a=60$ tadpoles killed and $b=120$ tadpoles per tank from a plot of these
data, which correspond to $\alpha=0.5$ per experiment and $H=1/60$ experiments per tadpole
killed. We give them to `MakeADFun()` on the transformed scales and fit the model:

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process the NLL, starting from the values read by eye in Chapter 5.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)

# Minimise the NLL with BFGS and check the convergence code.
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_fit$convergence
```

The estimates are transformed back to the original scale. By invariance
([Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-constraints)), the estimates of other quantities of
the curve follow from them. Two are useful here: the largest number of tadpoles that the
larvae could kill in one experiment, $1/H$, which is the asymptote of the expected number
killed, and the density at which the expected number killed reaches half of that
asymptote, $1/(\alpha H)$ (the parameters $a$ and $b$ of the Michaelis–Menten form):

```{r}
# Estimates on the original scale.
alpha_mle = unname(plogis(binomial_fit$par["logit_alpha"]))
H_mle = unname(exp(binomial_fit$par["log_H"]))

# Asymptote and half-maximum of the expected number killed, by invariance.
c(
  alpha_mle = alpha_mle,
  H_mle = H_mle,
  max_killed = 1 / H_mle,
  half_maximum = 1 / (alpha_mle * H_mle)
)
```

The estimates are $\hat\alpha\approx0.526$ per experiment and $\hat H\approx0.0166$
experiments per tadpole killed. The larvae could kill at most about 60 tadpoles in one
experiment, and the expected number killed reaches half of this at about 115 tadpoles per
tank. These values are close to the 60 and 120 that Chapter 5 read by eye
(@fig-fitted_curve), which is not surprising: the initial slope of the curve can be read
from the tanks at low density, and the asymptote that Chapter 5 chose happened to be close
to the estimate. Chapter 5 also found that these data say little about the asymptote, and
@sec-curve-uncertainty shows what this means for the uncertainty of the estimates.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-fitted_curve
#| fig-cap: "Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points), with the expected number killed under the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted by maximum likelihood (solid line) and with the values read by eye in Chapter 5 (dashed line)."
# Expected number killed with the maximum likelihood estimates and with the values by eye.
initial_values = seq(from = 0, to = 100, length.out = 200)
fitted_curves = data.frame(
  initial = rep(initial_values, times = 2),
  killed = c(
    initial_values * alpha_mle / (1 + alpha_mle * H_mle * initial_values),
    initial_values * alpha_eye / (1 + alpha_eye * H_eye * initial_values)
  ),
  curve = rep(c("Maximum likelihood", "By eye (Chapter 5)"), each = length(initial_values))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = ReedfrogFuncresp,
    aes(x = Initial, y = Killed),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = fitted_curves,
    aes(x = initial, y = killed, linetype = curve),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Maximum likelihood" = "solid", "By eye (Chapter 5)" = "dashed")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Initial number of tadpoles per tank",
    y = "Tadpoles killed in 14 days",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A convergence code of zero is the first check of a fit. The next is whether the fitted
model describes the data, which we check with residuals in @sec-response-residuals. When the
code is not zero, the note "When a fit fails" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-constraints) says what to try.

## The gradient and automatic differentiation {#sec-makeadfun}

Since [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-maximum-likelihood) we have given every NLL to
`MakeADFun()` before fitting it. There we said that this step processes the NLL so that the
tools of the course can work with it, and that RTMB supplies the slope that BFGS uses. We
can now say what that slope is. The **gradient** of the NLL is the vector of its partial
derivatives with respect to the parameters
([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-parameter-derivatives)), that is, its slope in the
direction of each parameter. RTMB calculates it by **automatic differentiation**: from the
code of the NLL, exactly up to rounding error, and without a formula from us. The element
`gr` of the object returns the gradient at the parameter values that we give it, on the
scale that is optimised, with one column per parameter in the order of the list of
parameters:

```{r}
# The gradient of the NLL at the starting values and at the estimates.
binomial_obj$gr(binomial_obj$par)
binomial_obj$gr(binomial_fit$par)
```

At the starting values the gradient is not zero, and its signs tell BFGS in which
direction to move each parameter to lower the NLL. At the estimates both elements are
close to zero, as they should be at a minimum.

An exact gradient matters for response curves for three reasons. First, BFGS uses the
gradient at every step to decide in which direction to move. Without `gr`, `optim()`
approximates it by evaluating the NLL at nearby values of every parameter
([Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd#sec-gradients) explains how), which costs time and accuracy. Second,
the parameters of a curve are often correlated, as we will see in @sec-curve-uncertainty,
so that the NLL forms a narrow and tilted valley like the one of the owl model in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-surface). In such a valley the direction
of the next step depends on small differences between the partial derivatives, and an
inexact gradient can stop the search before it reaches the minimum. Third, the same
derivatives are behind the other tools of the course: `sdreport()` calculates the curvature
of the NLL from them, `ADREPORT()` uses them for the standard errors of quantities
calculated from the parameters (@sec-delta-method), and in
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) they are needed to integrate random effects out of the
likelihood.

For RTMB to calculate these derivatives, the NLL must be written with operations and
functions that RTMB knows. This is the reason why the probability mass and density
functions of the course come from RTMB and RTMBdist.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Technical detail: how automatic differentiation works"}
[RTMB](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RTMB/vignettes/RTMB-introduction.html) is an
R interface to the package Template Model Builder (TMB). `MakeADFun()` runs the NLL once, at
the starting values, and records every elementary operation that the function carries out on
the parameters (each sum, product, division, exponential and logarithm), in the order in
which they happen. This record is called a **tape**. The derivative of each of these
operations is known (they are the
[rules of differentiation](../Supplements/calculus.qmd#sec-calc-rules)), and the chain rule
combines them along the tape into the derivative of the NLL with respect to every parameter.
In plain English, RTMB differentiates the code of the NLL step by step, as we would
differentiate a formula by hand. The result is exact up to rounding error: it is neither an
algebraic formula nor a numerical approximation. The elements `fn`, `gr` and `he` (the
Hessian) of the object all work from the tape. Because the tape runs through TMB's compiled
code, it cannot be stepped through like ordinary R code.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="When automatic differentiation needs care"}
RTMB works out the derivatives from the calculations that the NLL carried out when
`MakeADFun()` ran it at the starting values, so every calculation that involves a parameter
must have a derivative. A branch that depends on a parameter (an `if` that compares a
parameter with a value) does not: if it were recorded, only the side taken at the starting
values would be used afterwards. RTMB therefore refuses such a comparison, and `MakeADFun()`
stops with the error "Comparison is generally unsafe for AD types". In the same way, a curve
with a sharp change at an unknown threshold has no derivative at the change. Such
[calculations need special care](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RTMB/vignettes/RTMB-tips.html),
and a smooth curve that approximates the sharp change is the usual solution.
Check the NLL on sensible parameter values in R first (a function written with `getAll()`
can be called directly with two lists), and inspect `binomial_obj$fn(binomial_obj$par)` and
`binomial_obj$gr(binomial_obj$par)` before fitting.
:::

# Uncertainty of a response curve {#sec-curve-uncertainty}

The uncertainty of the estimates is calculated from the likelihood, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty). Two questions are new
with a response curve. The first is how the precision of each parameter depends on where
the observations lie along the predictor. The second is how uncertain the curve itself is,
since a point of the curve is a quantity calculated from all of its parameters.

## Standard errors and correlation of the parameters

`sdreport()` calculates the standard errors and the covariance matrix of the estimates from
the curvature of the NLL, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-automation). Two features are typical of the
parameters of a curve. Their estimates are often strongly correlated, because different
combinations of the parameters give similar curves over the range of the data. And how
precisely each parameter is estimated depends on where along $x$ the observations lie.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-parameter-derivatives) showed with partial
derivatives that a curve responds to each parameter in a different part of its range; the
observations that inform a parameter are those made where the curve responds to it. So data
that cover only the rise of a saturating curve determine its initial slope better than its
asymptote. The correlation also depends on the parameterisation, whereas the fit does not
(see "Parameterisation, slices and profiles" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-surface)).

For the tanks, `summary()` gives the estimates and standard errors on the optimised scales,
and `cov2cor()` turns the covariance matrix in the element `cov.fixed` into correlations:

```{r}
# Standard errors on the optimised scales, and the correlation between the estimates.
binomial_sd = sdreport(binomial_obj)
summary(binomial_sd)
cov2cor(binomial_sd$cov.fixed)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The same model in the Michaelis–Menten form, with a = 1 / H and b = 1 / (alpha * H):
# the same maximum, and a higher correlation between the estimates of log(a) and log(b).
mm_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  p = a / (b + initial)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
mm_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(mm_nll, frog_data),
  list(log_a = log(60), log_b = log(120)),
  silent = TRUE
)
mm_fit = optim(par = mm_obj$par, fn = mm_obj$fn, gr = mm_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = mm_fit$convergence, nll = mm_fit$value, nll_holling = binomial_fit$value)
exp(mm_fit$par)
cov2cor(sdreport(mm_obj)$cov.fixed)
```

The correlation between the estimates of $\operatorname{logit}(\alpha)$ and $\log(H)$ is
0.82. It is positive because a steeper initial rise of the curve (a larger $\alpha$) must
be compensated by a stronger levelling off (a larger $H$) for the curve to pass through the
tanks at high density, so hypothetical samples that overestimate one parameter tend to
overestimate the other. In the Michaelis–Menten form, with $\log(a)$ and $\log(b)$, the
same model has the same maximum and a correlation of 0.98: the estimates of the asymptote
and of the half-maximum are almost interchangeable, because the data determine mainly their
ratio, the initial slope $a/b=\alpha$. This is what Chapter 5 found when it read starting
values from these data ("Starting values by eye"). The densities of the experiment stop at
100 tadpoles per tank, below the estimated half-maximum of 115, so the tanks cover less than
half of the rise of the curve. They determine $\alpha$, which describes the start of the
curve, much better than $H$, which describes its end, as the intervals of the next section
show.

## Likelihood profile intervals of the parameters

Likelihood profile intervals are calculated with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()`, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-profile_intervals), and they remain the reference
method. With a response curve, the profile of a poorly determined parameter is often
asymmetric, because the data rule out values on one side of the estimate much more
strongly than on the other. The endpoints of the interval can be transformed with any
monotonic function to give an interval for a quantity calculated from the parameter: an
increasing function keeps their order and a decreasing function swaps them. We profile both
parameters, transform the endpoints back, and calculate the interval of the largest number
of tadpoles killed, $1/H$, from that of $H$:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profiles of logit(alpha) and log(H). Each profile contains the estimate twice, so
# confint() warns that it collapses repeated values; the warning can be ignored.
binomial_profile_alpha = TMB::tmbprofile(binomial_obj, name = "logit_alpha", trace = FALSE)
binomial_profile_H = TMB::tmbprofile(binomial_obj, name = "log_H", trace = FALSE)

# 95% intervals transformed back to the original scale.
alpha_interval = plogis(confint(binomial_profile_alpha))
H_interval = exp(confint(binomial_profile_H))

# 1 / H decreases with H, so the endpoints swap.
profile_intervals = rbind(alpha_interval, H_interval, rev(1 / H_interval))
dimnames(profile_intervals) = list(c("alpha", "H", "1/H"), c("lower", "upper"))
profile_intervals
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# Wald interval of H from the log scale, and the corresponding interval of 1 / H.
binomial_summary = summary(binomial_sd)
wald_H = exp(
  binomial_summary["log_H", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * binomial_summary["log_H", "Std. Error"]
)
rev(1 / wald_H)
```

The interval for the attack rate, 0.40 to 0.68 per experiment, is narrow compared with the
interval for the handling time, which spans almost a factor of four. Accordingly, the
interval for the largest number of tadpoles that the larvae could kill in one experiment
runs from 38 to 143 around an estimate of 60: it extends 22 tadpoles below the estimate and
83 above it, and its upper end lies beyond the largest density of the experiment. The data
rule out a low asymptote, because the larvae killed up to 35 tadpoles, but not a high one.
The profile is asymmetric even on the log scale, so the Wald interval from the log scale (34
to 107 tadpoles) misses most of the upper part of the profile interval.

## Uncertainty of the fitted curve {#sec-delta-method}

A point of the curve, such as the expected number killed at a given density, is a quantity
calculated from the parameters. Its standard error is requested with `ADREPORT()`, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-constrained), where TMB applies the delta
method (the box below gives the formula for several parameters). `ADREPORT()` of a vector
reports every element with its own standard error, so if we pass a grid of predictor values
in the list of data and calculate the curve on that grid inside the NLL, `sdreport()`
returns the curve and its standard error at every point of the grid. From them we calculate
a Wald interval at each point, on a scale on which the quantity is unbounded, and transform
the endpoints back, for the same reasons as for the parameters in Chapter 4. For a
probability that scale is the logit. Together the intervals form a **confidence band**.

The band is **pointwise**: at each value of $x$, the interval contains the value of the curve
under the data generating process at that $x$ in approximately 95% of hypothetical samples. This is not the same as a
band that contains the whole curve in 95% of hypothetical samples, which would be wider.
The band also says nothing about where the observations of new tanks would fall: that is
described by the distribution of the observations around the curve
(@fig-curve_distribution), which is much wider.

For the reed frogs we add a grid of densities from 0 to 100 tadpoles per tank to the list of
data, as `initial_grid`:

```{r}
# A grid of densities (tadpoles per tank), added to the list of data.
initial_grid = seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 1)
frog_data$initial_grid = initial_grid
```

The NLL gains three lines, which calculate the probability that a tadpole is killed at
every density of the grid, its logit with `qlogis()`, and ask for the standard error of
every element with `ADREPORT()`. We process the new NLL, fit it again (the estimates do not
change) and call `sdreport()`:

```{r}
# The Binomial NLL with three more lines.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  # The logit of the probability of being killed at every density of the grid.
  p_grid = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial_grid)
  logit_p_grid = qlogis(p_grid)
  ADREPORT(logit_p_grid)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_sd = sdreport(binomial_obj)
```

With the argument `select = "report"`, `summary()` returns only the rows of the quantities
requested with `ADREPORT()`, here one row per density of the grid. We calculate the Wald
interval of each row on the logit scale, transform the endpoints back with `plogis()` and
multiply them by the density to obtain the band for the expected number killed:

```{r}
# Rows of logit_p_grid: one per density of the grid.
band_summary = summary(binomial_sd, select = "report")

# Wald intervals on the logit scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
logit_lower = band_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]
logit_upper = band_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# The curve and its band for the expected number killed.
curve_band = data.frame(
  initial = initial_grid,
  killed = initial_grid * plogis(band_summary[, "Estimate"]),
  lower = initial_grid * plogis(logit_lower),
  upper = initial_grid * plogis(logit_upper)
)
```

@fig-curve_band shows the band with the data, the formula of the model and the estimates.
On the logit scale the band is narrowest near 50 tadpoles per tank and wider towards both
ends. The tanks at low density hold few tadpoles each, so most of the information about the
curve comes from the denser tanks, and the band widens away from the middle of that
information. For the expected number
killed the band also widens with density because the probability is multiplied by the number
of tadpoles; at the highest density it runs from about 24 to 33 tadpoles killed. So within
the range of the data the curve is well determined, although its asymptote is not. Beyond
100 tadpoles per tank the band would widen quickly, because there the curve depends more and
more on the asymptote.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the delta method for several parameters"}
Let $g(\boldsymbol\theta)$ be a quantity calculated from the vector of parameters
$\boldsymbol\theta$ (on the scale that was optimised), such as the logit of the curve at one
density. Close to the estimates, the function $g$ is replaced by its tangent plane, the
extension of the tangent line of the one-parameter case to several parameters. The variance
of a linear function of the estimates follows from their covariance matrix, which gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\right)\approx
\nabla g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})^{\top}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\,
\nabla g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}),
$$

where $\nabla g$ is the gradient of $g$, the vector of its partial derivatives with respect
to each parameter ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-parameter-derivatives)),
evaluated at the estimates; $\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ is the covariance matrix of the
estimates, the element `cov.fixed` of `sdreport()`; and $^{\top}$ turns the column of
partial derivatives into a row. For two parameters the product is

$$
\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_1}\right)^2\hat\sigma_1^2+
\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_2}\right)^2\hat\sigma_2^2+
2\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_1}\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_2}\,\hat\sigma_{12},
$$

where $\hat\sigma_1^2$ and $\hat\sigma_2^2$ are the variances of the two estimates and
$\hat\sigma_{12}$ their covariance. In plain English, each parameter contributes its
variance multiplied by the square of the slope of $g$ in its direction, and each pair of
parameters contributes its covariance multiplied by the two slopes. With one parameter only
the first term remains, and its square root is the formula of the box on the delta method
in [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-constrained). For the curve of the reed frogs
a larger $\alpha$ raises the curve and a larger $H$ lowers it, so the two slopes have
opposite signs. Their estimates are positively correlated, so the last term is negative:
the two errors partly cancel on the curve, which is estimated more precisely than the
separate standard errors suggest.

RTMB calculates $\nabla g$ by automatic differentiation (@sec-makeadfun), which is why
`ADREPORT()` is called inside the NLL: the quantity has to be calculated there for RTMB to
differentiate it. The approximation is good when $g$ is close to a plane over the range of
parameter values that the uncertainty of the estimates covers. It is poor when $g$ bends
noticeably over that range, which happens when the standard errors are large (in small
samples) and when the quantity is close to a bound of its range on the scale on which it is
calculated; this is why the band is calculated on the logit scale.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curve_band
#| fig-cap: "Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points), with the expected number killed under the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted by maximum likelihood (line) and its pointwise 95% confidence band (shaded), calculated from Wald intervals on the logit scale. The inset gives the model, the estimates and their 95% likelihood profile intervals; α is per experiment, H in experiments per tadpole killed and 1/H in tadpoles killed per experiment."
# Model, estimates and profile intervals for the inset.
format_interval = function(estimate, interval, digits) {
  paste0(
    formatC(estimate, format = "f", digits = digits),
    " [", formatC(interval[1], format = "f", digits = digits),
    ", ", formatC(interval[2], format = "f", digits = digits), "]"
  )
}
model_inset = paste(
  "Model: K ~ Binomial(N, p(N))",
  "p(N) = α / (1 + α H N)",
  "",
  "Estimates (95% profile intervals):",
  paste("α =", format_interval(alpha_mle, profile_intervals["alpha", ], 3)),
  paste("H =", format_interval(H_mle, profile_intervals["H", ], 4)),
  paste("1/H =", format_interval(1 / H_mle, profile_intervals["1/H", ], 1)),
  sep = "\n"
)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = curve_band,
    aes(x = initial, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill = "#D55E00",
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = curve_band,
    aes(x = initial, y = killed),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ReedfrogFuncresp,
    aes(x = Initial, y = Killed),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    x = 0,
    y = 42,
    label = model_inset,
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    size = 3.2,
    fill = "grey99",
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 42)) +
  labs(x = "Initial number of tadpoles per tank", y = "Tadpoles killed in 14 days") +
  theme_classic()
```

Whether these intervals have a coverage close to 95% with 16 tanks can be checked by
simulation, in the same way as in "Coverage checked by simulation" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty); the extra exercise of the
[practical](Practicals/no_solution.qmd) does this for a quantity of a fitted curve.

:::: {#imp-ladybird-handling .callout-important title="handling time of a ladybird"}

A Holling type II curve is fitted to the number of aphids eaten by ladybird larvae in one
hour, with the handling time $H$ (hours per aphid) optimised on the log scale. The fit gives
$\log(\hat H)=-3.2$, and `sdreport()` gives a standard error of 0.20 for it. Calculate a 95%
Wald interval for $H$, and from it an interval for the largest number of aphids that a
larva can eat per hour, $1/H$. Why are the endpoints swapped in the second interval?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

We calculate the interval on the log scale, transform its endpoints with `exp()`, and then
take the inverse of both endpoints:

```{r}
# Wald interval for H (hours per aphid), from the log scale.
H_wald = exp(-3.2 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * 0.20)
H_wald

# Interval for 1 / H (aphids/hour): the inverse of the two endpoints, in reverse order.
rev(1 / H_wald)
```

The interval for $H$ goes from approximately 0.028 to 0.060 hours per aphid, and the
interval for the largest feeding rate from approximately 17 to 36 aphids/hour. The function $1/H$ decreases as $H$ increases, so the
lower endpoint of $H$ gives the upper endpoint of $1/H$, and the other way round.

:::
::::

# Checking the fitted model {#sec-response-residuals}

A fitted model describes the whole distribution of every observation, and not only its
expected value. **Checking** the model means comparing that description with the data. In
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd) the observations had a common distribution, so we
could compare their empirical distribution with the model distribution. With a response
curve each observation has a distribution of its own, and only one observation comes from
each of them. We therefore simulate many values from the distribution of each observation
and see where the observed value falls among them.

## Simulating from the fitted model

With its parameters at the estimates, a fitted model is a data generating process from which
we can simulate. As in "Coverage checked by simulation" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty), we mark the response with
`OBS()` inside the NLL, and the function `simulate()` of the processed object then draws one
hypothetical sample for the parameter values that we give it. A hypothetical sample has the
same design as the data: the same observations, with the same values of the predictor. Each
simulated value is drawn from the distribution of its observation, so the simulation
contains the variation of the observations around the curve, which is what the check needs.

For the reed frogs, the NLL gains one line, `killed = OBS(killed)`. We process it and fit it
again (the estimates do not change):

```{r}
# The Binomial NLL with one more line.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the response as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  killed = OBS(killed)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  p_grid = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial_grid)
  logit_p_grid = qlogis(p_grid)
  ADREPORT(logit_p_grid)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL and fit it again.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_fit$convergence
```

Each call to `simulate()` returns the numbers killed in 16 simulated tanks with the initial
numbers of the experiment. We store 1,000 hypothetical samples in a matrix with one row per
tank and one column per hypothetical sample:

```{r}
# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 16 tanks at the estimates: one row per tank and one
# column per hypothetical sample.
n_sim = 1000
binomial_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(frog_data$killed), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 601)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  binomial_simulations[, j] = binomial_obj$simulate(binomial_fit$par)$killed
}

# The first five hypothetical samples of the first four tanks (5, 5, 10 and 10 tadpoles).
binomial_simulations[1:4, 1:5]
```

## Scaled quantile residuals

The **scaled quantile residual** of an observation is the fraction of its simulated values
that are smaller than the observed value. An observation in the middle of its simulated
values has a residual close to 0.5, one below all of them a residual of 0 and one above all
of them a residual of 1. For a discrete response, the observed value is often equal to some
of the simulated values, and the residual is then drawn at random between the fraction of
simulated values that are smaller and the fraction that are smaller or equal. If the model
describes the data generating process, each observation behaves like one more draw from its
own distribution, so it is equally likely to fall anywhere among its simulated values. The
residuals are then approximately uniform between 0 and 1, whatever the distribution of the
observations and whatever the values of the predictor. This is what makes them useful for
response curves: they put observations with different distributions on one common
scale.^[Dunn and Smyth (1996) defined these residuals from the cumulative probability
function of the model and transformed them to the scale of a standard Normal distribution:
Dunn, P. K. and Smyth, G. K. (1996), "Randomized quantile residuals", *Journal of
Computational and Graphical Statistics* 5: 236–244. The package DHARMa calculates them from
simulations and keeps them between 0 and 1: Hartig, F. (2026), *DHARMa: Residual
diagnostics for hierarchical (multi-level / mixed) regression models*, R package version
0.5.0.]

Three kinds of pattern show that the model disagrees with the data:

- a distribution of the residuals that is not uniform: too many residuals near 0 and 1 mean
  that the observations vary more around the curve than the model allows, and too many near
  0.5 that they vary less;
- a trend of the residuals against the predictor or against the fitted values, which means
  that the curve misses a systematic change of the response;
- residuals of exactly 0 or 1, from observations outside the range of all their simulated
  values, which DHARMa marks as outliers.

The function `DHARMa::createDHARMa()` calculates the residuals from simulations that we
supply. Its arguments are:

- `simulatedResponse`, the matrix of simulated values, with one row per observation;
- `observedResponse`, the observed values;
- `fittedPredictedResponse`, the expected value of each observation under the fitted model,
  which DHARMa uses in its plots and in the dispersion statistic below;
- `integerResponse = TRUE` for a discrete response, so that ties are drawn at random as
  described above.

`plot()` of the result draws two panels: on the left a quantile–quantile plot of the
residuals against a uniform distribution, and on the right the residuals against the
fitted values, on the scale of their ranks, with the quartiles 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 as
dashed lines. `DHARMa::plotResiduals()` with the argument `form` draws the residuals against
any predictor. For the reed frogs the expected number killed increases with the initial
number of tadpoles, so the right panel already shows the residuals in the order of the
densities. We calculate the expected number killed in each tank and the residuals:

```{r}
#| label: fig-residuals_binomial
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted to the 16 tanks, from 1,000 hypothetical samples, as drawn by DHARMa. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals against the rank of the expected number killed, with the quartiles of a uniform distribution (dashed lines) and lines fitted to the quartiles of the residuals. The star marks a tank whose observed number lies outside the range of its simulated values."
# Expected number killed in each tank under the fitted model.
binomial_expected = frog_data$initial * alpha_mle /
  (1 + alpha_mle * H_mle * frog_data$initial)

# Scaled quantile residuals from the simulations, and the two standard panels.
binomial_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = binomial_simulations,
  observedResponse = frog_data$killed,
  fittedPredictedResponse = binomial_expected,
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
plot(binomial_residuals)
```

The residuals do not follow a uniform distribution: in the quantile–quantile plot the upper
half of the residuals lies above the line, so more tanks than expected have residuals close
to 1, and one tank, with 50 tadpoles of which 5 were killed, lies below all its simulated
values (the star). In the right panel the lines fitted to the quartiles of the residuals
lie on or outside the dashed lines, the upper one well above 0.75: the tanks spread further from
the middle of their simulated values than the model allows. There is no clear trend against
density, so the curve itself does not miss a systematic change.

DHARMa summarises the spread with a **dispersion statistic**: the variance of the observed
values around their expected values, divided by the average of the same variance in the
simulated samples. It is close to one when the model allows the right amount of variation.
The function `DHARMa::testDispersion()` calculates it; we keep only its element `statistic`:

```{r}
# Observed spread around the curve relative to the simulated spread.
DHARMa::testDispersion(binomial_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
```

The numbers killed vary around the curve almost three times as much (as a variance) as the
Binomial model allows. This is **overdispersion** relative to the Binomial distribution,
which [Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd) introduced for counts relative to the Poisson
distribution ("Overdispersion"). The two tanks with 50 tadpoles, with 5 and 21 killed, show
it in the data: under the Binomial model they share the same distribution, in which 5
killed is very unlikely. The model assumes that every tadpole of a tank has the same
probability of being killed, independently of the other tadpoles, and these tanks differ
more than that assumption allows.

DHARMa also prints tests with p-values, on its plots and in functions such as
`testDispersion()`. We read the plots and the dispersion statistic as exploratory evidence
and do not rest decisions on the p-values, for the reasons given in
[Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) and at the end of
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic): with 16 tanks a large p-value mainly says
that there are few data, and a small one does not say how much the disagreement matters.

::: {.callout-warning title="What a residual check can and cannot show"}
A residual check shows where a fitted model disagrees with the data. It does not say which
assumption is wrong: overdispersion can come from the distribution, from a predictor that is
missing from the curve, or from observations that are not independent. Nor does a plot
without a pattern show that the model is right or that the observations are independent;
with few observations only large disagreements are visible.
:::

# A model for overdispersed proportions {#sec-beta-binomial-fit}

When the probability of an outcome varies among sampling units beyond what the predictor
explains, the counts vary more than a Binomial model allows. The
[Beta-Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-beta_binomial) distribution describes
this situation: the probability of each sampling unit is drawn from a Beta distribution,
and the count of that unit follows a Binomial distribution with this probability. With a
response curve we parameterise it with the mean probability $p$, which the curve gives,
and the **precision** $\kappa$ ($\kappa=a+b$ in the supplement, where $a$ and $b$ are the
shape parameters of the Beta distribution, and so $a=\kappa p$ and $b=\kappa(1-p)$). For a
unit with $N$ trials the mean and the variance of the count are

$$
E[K]=Np,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(K)=Np(1-p)\,\frac{\kappa+N}{\kappa+1},
$$

where $Np(1-p)$ is the variance of a Binomial distribution with the same mean. The factor
$(\kappa+N)/(\kappa+1)$ is larger than one whenever $N>1$ and approaches one as $\kappa$
grows, so a small $\kappa$ means much variation among units and a large $\kappa$ gives
almost a Binomial distribution. Note that the factor grows with $N$: the variation of the
probability among units matters more when each unit has more trials. The precision is
positive, so we optimise $\log(\kappa)$.

The curve does not change: only the observation model is revised, so that the probability
that a tadpole is killed varies among tanks around $p(N)$. This is the step of the modelling
cycle of [Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) in which a check sends us back to the model.
For the tanks,

$$
K_i \sim \operatorname{Beta-Binomial}\left(N_i,\,\kappa\,p(N_i),\,\kappa\left(1-p(N_i)\right)\right),
\qquad
p(N)=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha HN}.
$$

The NLL uses `dbetabinom()` of RTMBdist, whose arguments `shape1` and `shape2` are the two
shape parameters. We include `OBS()` from the start, because we will check this model too:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Beta-Binomial model with the Holling type II curve.
betabinomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  killed = OBS(killed)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  kappa = exp(log_kappa)
  # Mean probability that a tadpole is killed, at the density of each tank.
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  -sum(dbetabinom(
    x = killed, size = initial, shape1 = kappa * p, shape2 = kappa * (1 - p), log = TRUE
  ))
}
```

We start from the estimates of the Binomial model and a precision of 10, fit the model and
calculate the standard errors:

```{r}
# Process the NLL, starting from the Binomial estimates and kappa = 10, and fit it.
betabinomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(betabinomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(
    logit_alpha = binomial_fit$par[["logit_alpha"]],
    log_H = binomial_fit$par[["log_H"]],
    log_kappa = log(10)
  ),
  silent = TRUE
)
betabinomial_fit = optim(
  par = betabinomial_obj$par,
  fn = betabinomial_obj$fn,
  gr = betabinomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
betabinomial_fit$convergence

# Standard errors on the optimised scales, and the estimates on the original scale.
betabinomial_sd = sdreport(betabinomial_obj)
summary(betabinomial_sd)
alpha_bb = plogis(betabinomial_fit$par[["logit_alpha"]])
H_bb = exp(betabinomial_fit$par[["log_H"]])
c(alpha = alpha_bb, H = H_bb, kappa = exp(betabinomial_fit$par[["log_kappa"]]))
```

The estimates of the curve hardly change ($\hat\alpha\approx0.54$ per experiment against
0.53 under the Binomial model, and $\hat H\approx0.018$ against 0.017 experiments per
tadpole killed), but their standard errors on the optimised scales are larger: 0.38 against
0.29 for $\operatorname{logit}(\hat\alpha)$ and 0.46 against 0.29 for $\log(\hat H)$. The
Binomial model treated every tadpole as an independent trial, so it took the tanks as more
informative than they are. When the probability varies among tanks, the tadpoles of a tank
share part of their fate, and the information about the curve depends more on the number
of tanks than on the number of tadpoles. So the standard errors of the Binomial model were
too small. The estimated precision, $\hat\kappa\approx26$, gives a variance factor of about
1.3 for a tank with 10 tadpoles and about 4.6 for a tank with 100 tadpoles.

To check the revised model we repeat the simulation and the residuals with the new object:

```{r}
# 1,000 hypothetical samples from the fitted Beta-Binomial model.
betabinomial_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(frog_data$killed), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 602)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  betabinomial_simulations[, j] = betabinomial_obj$simulate(betabinomial_fit$par)$killed
}

# Residuals and dispersion statistic.
betabinomial_expected = frog_data$initial * alpha_bb /
  (1 + alpha_bb * H_bb * frog_data$initial)
betabinomial_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = betabinomial_simulations,
  observedResponse = frog_data$killed,
  fittedPredictedResponse = betabinomial_expected,
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
DHARMa::testDispersion(betabinomial_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
```

The dispersion statistic is now close to one, and the tank with 5 of 50 tadpoles killed lies
within the range of its simulated values: the Beta-Binomial model allows about as much
variation among tanks as the data show.

:::: {#imp-fruit-set .callout-important title="fruit set in inflorescences"}

Each inflorescence of a shrub has 20 flowers, and the mean probability that a flower sets
fruit is 0.4. Calculate the variance of the number of fruits per inflorescence under a
Binomial model and under a Beta-Binomial model with $\kappa=5$. Which value of $\kappa$
would make the variance of the Beta-Binomial model only 10% larger than that of the
Binomial model? Verify the variance for $\kappa=5$ in R from the probability mass.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The Binomial variance is $20\times0.4\times0.6=4.8$. With $\kappa=5$ the factor is
$(5+20)/(5+1)\approx4.17$, so the variance is $4.8\times25/6=20$, more than four
times larger. For a variance 10% larger the factor must be 1.1:
$(\kappa+20)/(\kappa+1)=1.1$ gives $\kappa+20=1.1\kappa+1.1$, so $\kappa=189$. In R, the
variance is the sum of the squared distances from the mean (8 fruits) weighted by the
probability mass, with shape parameters $5\times0.4=2$ and $5\times0.6=3$:

```{r}
# Variance of the Beta-Binomial model from its probability mass.
fruit_values = 0:20
sum((fruit_values - 8)^2 * dbetabinom(x = fruit_values, size = 20, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 3))
```

:::
::::

# Comparing candidate models {#sec-response-comparison}

The candidate models of a comparison should represent plausible ecological or statistical
alternatives, and they must all be fitted to the same observations: the same rows, the same
response and the same units. Often some candidates are nested in others: a model is nested
in another when it is the special case obtained by fixing a parameter of the other at a
particular value, as for the curves of
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions).

For the reed frogs we have two questions. Does the probability that a tadpole is killed
decrease with density? And do the tanks vary more than a Binomial model allows? Each
question gives two alternatives, and together they give four candidates:

| Curve | Binomial | Beta-Binomial |
|---|---|---|
| Constant probability, $p(N)=\alpha$ | $\alpha$ ($K=1$) | $\alpha$, $\kappa$ ($K=2$) |
| Holling type II, $p(N)=\alpha/(1+\alpha HN)$ | $\alpha$, $H$ ($K=2$) | $\alpha$, $H$, $\kappa$ ($K=3$) |

: The four candidate models and their parameters. $K$ is the number of parameters.

The constant probability is the Holling type II curve with $H=0$: the larvae kill the same
fraction of the tadpoles at every density, so the expected number killed, $\alpha N$,
increases in proportion to the density. The Binomial distribution is the limit of the
Beta-Binomial distribution as $\kappa$ grows without bound. So the model with a constant
probability and a Binomial distribution is nested in each of the others, and each Binomial
model is nested in the Beta-Binomial model with the same curve. The Holling type II curve
with a Binomial distribution and the constant probability with a Beta-Binomial distribution
are not nested in each other, but they can still be compared, because they are fitted to the
same observations. The special values $H=0$ and $\kappa=\infty$ cannot be reached on the
optimised scales (they would be $\log(H)=-\infty$ and $\log(\kappa)=\infty$), so the two
models with a constant probability have NLLs of their own:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihoods of the two models with a constant probability.
constant_binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = alpha, log = TRUE))
}

constant_betabinomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  kappa = exp(log_kappa)
  -sum(dbetabinom(
    x = killed, size = initial, shape1 = kappa * alpha, shape2 = kappa * (1 - alpha),
    log = TRUE
  ))
}
```

We fit the four models in the same way, so we write a small function that processes an NLL
for a list of data and minimises it from the starting values that we give it, and a list
with the NLL and the starting values of every candidate (the values read by eye in Chapter 5
and a precision of 10):

```{r}
# Fit one model to one list of data, from the given starting values.
fit_model = function(nll, start, data) {
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(nll, data), start, silent = TRUE)
  optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
}

# The NLL and the starting values of each candidate.
models = list(
  constant_binomial = list(
    nll = constant_binomial_nll,
    start = list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5))
  ),
  holling_binomial = list(
    nll = binomial_nll,
    start = list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60))
  ),
  constant_betabinomial = list(
    nll = constant_betabinomial_nll,
    start = list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_kappa = log(10))
  ),
  holling_betabinomial = list(
    nll = betabinomial_nll,
    start = list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60), log_kappa = log(10))
  )
)
```

A loop fits the four candidates to the 16 tanks and stores, for each of them, the number of
parameters, the maximum log-likelihood (minus the element `value` of the fit) and the
convergence code:

```{r}
# Fit every candidate to the 16 tanks.
comparison = data.frame(model = names(models), K = NA, loglik = NA, convergence = NA)
for (m in seq_along(models)) {
  fit = fit_model(models[[m]]$nll, models[[m]]$start, frog_data)
  comparison$K[m] = length(fit$par)
  comparison$loglik[m] = -fit$value
  comparison$convergence[m] = fit$convergence
}
comparison
```

All four fits converged. As it must be for nested models, the maximum log-likelihood is
highest for the model with the most parameters, which is why we need criteria that take the
number of parameters into account.

## Information criteria

[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic) introduced AIC and its corrected version AICc,

$$
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
\qquad
\mathrm{AICc}=\mathrm{AIC}+\frac{2K(K+1)}{n-K-1},
$$

where $K$ is the number of estimated parameters, $n$ the number of observations and
$\ell(\hat\theta)$ the maximum log-likelihood, in which $\hat\theta$ stands for all the
estimated parameters of the model (here those of $\boldsymbol\beta$ and any shared
parameter). With 16 observations and up to three
parameters the correction of AICc is not negligible. The **Bayesian information criterion**
(BIC)^[Schwarz, G. (1978), "Estimating the dimension of a model", *Annals of Statistics* 6:
461–464. The name comes from its derivation, as a large-sample approximation in Bayesian
inference, but it is used in the same way as AIC.] has a penalty that grows with the number
of observations:

$$
\mathrm{BIC}=K\log(n)-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
$$

with the same symbols. Each parameter costs $\log(n)$ units instead of two, which is more
than two when $n$ is larger than $e^2\approx7.4$, so for most data sets BIC penalises
additional parameters more strongly than AIC. The two criteria also have different aims.
AIC estimates how well the fitted model would predict new data from the same process. BIC
tends, as the sample grows, to select the model with the fewest parameters among the
candidates that contain the data generating process. So in large samples BIC tends to
prefer simpler models than AIC does, and the two criteria can rank the same candidates
differently. Like AIC, BIC is used as a difference between models fitted to the same
observations, the lowest value is preferred, and it ranks the candidates without showing
that the best of them describes the data well.

In AICc and BIC, $n$ is the number of independent observations, which is the number of
tanks, 16, and not the 610 tadpoles that they contained: under the Beta-Binomial model the
tadpoles of a tank share the probability of that tank, so they are not independent
observations. The same $n$ must be used for every model that is compared. We add the three
criteria to the table:

```{r}
# AIC, AICc and BIC, with the number of tanks as the number of observations.
n_tanks = length(frog_data$killed)
comparison$aic = 2 * comparison$K - 2 * comparison$loglik
comparison$aicc = comparison$aic +
  2 * comparison$K * (comparison$K + 1) / (n_tanks - comparison$K - 1)
comparison$bic = comparison$K * log(n_tanks) - 2 * comparison$loglik
```

## Comparing the four models

Only differences between models matter for each criterion, so we calculate the difference
of each model from the one with the lowest value of that criterion:

```{r}
# Differences from the best model for each criterion.
data.frame(
  model = comparison$model,
  K = comparison$K,
  loglik = round(comparison$loglik, 2),
  delta_aic = round(comparison$aic - min(comparison$aic), 2),
  delta_aicc = round(comparison$aicc - min(comparison$aicc), 2),
  delta_bic = round(comparison$bic - min(comparison$bic), 2)
)
```

For the variation among tanks the criteria agree: with either curve, every criterion
prefers the Beta-Binomial model to the Binomial model, by 6.7 (Holling type II) and 13.0
(constant probability) units of AIC. This agrees with the residuals of
@sec-response-residuals.

For the density dependence of the risk the answer depends on the distribution. Under the
Binomial models, the Holling type II curve is clearly better than a constant probability (9.0
units of AIC). Under the Beta-Binomial models AIC, AICc and BIC still prefer the Holling type
II curve, but only by 2.7, 1.6 and 2.0 units. The Binomial models overstated the evidence
for density dependence for the same reason that they understated the standard errors: they
treated the tadpoles as independent trials. With 16 tanks that vary among themselves, the
data say clearly that a tadpole is killed with a probability of about one half at low
density, and that the tanks vary more than a Binomial model allows, but they hardly
distinguish a probability that decreases with density from a constant one over densities of
5 to 100 tadpoles per tank.

For the ecological answer we use the Beta-Binomial model with the Holling type II curve,
which all three criteria prefer by a small margin and which contains the constant
probability as the case $H=0$, and we calculate likelihood profile intervals for its
parameters as in @sec-curve-uncertainty:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profiles of logit(alpha) and log(H) of the Beta-Binomial model (confint() warns
# about repeated values, as before).
betabinomial_profile_alpha = TMB::tmbprofile(
  betabinomial_obj, name = "logit_alpha", trace = FALSE
)
betabinomial_profile_H = TMB::tmbprofile(betabinomial_obj, name = "log_H", trace = FALSE)

# 95% intervals on the original scale; 1 / H decreases with H, so the endpoints swap.
H_interval_bb = exp(confint(betabinomial_profile_H))
betabinomial_intervals = rbind(
  plogis(confint(betabinomial_profile_alpha)),
  H_interval_bb,
  rev(1 / H_interval_bb)
)
dimnames(betabinomial_intervals) = list(c("alpha", "H", "1/H"), c("lower", "upper"))
betabinomial_intervals
```

The attack rate is estimated at 0.54 per experiment, with an interval from 0.38 to 0.76: at
low density, between about two fifths and three quarters of the tadpoles are killed on
average in the 14 days. The handling time is estimated at 0.018 experiments per tadpole killed, but its
interval runs from 0.0019 to 0.038, so the largest number of tadpoles that three larvae
could kill in one experiment, about 56, has an interval from 27 to more than 500. The lower
end of the interval of $H$ is close to zero, which is the constant probability, and this
agrees with the comparison. The tanks rule out a low maximum but say little about how high
it is, as we found in @sec-curve-uncertainty, and allowing for the variation among tanks
widens the interval further. To estimate the handling time, an experiment would need tanks
with densities well above the half-maximum, where the curve levels off.

# A recipe for a response curve

The steps of this chapter extend the recipe of
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic) to models in which a curve describes a
parameter of the distribution of each observation:

::: {.callout-note title="A recipe for a response curve"}
1. Choose the curve from what is known about the process and from a plot of the data
   ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd)), and the observation model, with the parameter
   that the curve describes and the range that this parameter requires.
2. Write the NLL with the predictor and the response in the list of data, transforming
   every constrained parameter inside it.
3. Read starting values for the parameters of the curve from a plot of the data.
4. Fit the model with `MakeADFun()` and `optim()`, check that `convergence` is zero, and
   plot the fitted curve over the data.
5. Calculate standard errors and correlations with `sdreport()`, and likelihood profile
   intervals with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()` for the parameters that the question
   is about.
6. Calculate the curve on a grid of the predictor with `ADREPORT()`, and its confidence band
   from Wald intervals on a scale on which the curve is unbounded.
7. Mark the response with `OBS()`, simulate hypothetical samples with `obj$simulate()`, and
   check the scaled quantile residuals with DHARMa.
8. Revise the curve or the observation model where the residuals show a disagreement, and
   check the revised model in the same way.
9. Compare the candidate models, fitted to the same observations, with AIC, AICc and BIC.
10. Interpret the estimates and intervals of the preferred model in units, in terms of the
    ecological question, and say what the data leave uncertain.
:::

# Summary

A response curve describes one parameter of the distribution of each observation, usually
its mean or, for a Binomial distribution, its probability, as a function of a predictor. The
curve must return values in the range of that parameter. The observations are treated as
independent, but each has its own distribution. The log-likelihood is the sum of the log
probabilities of the observations, each calculated at its own value of the predictor, and it
is maximised with the tools of Chapter 4, with the predictor in the list of data and
starting values read from a plot. RTMB calculates the gradient of the NLL exactly by
automatic differentiation, which BFGS, `sdreport()` and `ADREPORT()` all rely on.

The parameters of a curve are often strongly correlated, and how precisely each of them is
estimated depends on where the observations lie along the predictor: observations inform a
parameter where the curve responds to it. Likelihood profile intervals follow the asymmetry
of a poorly determined parameter, and their endpoints can be transformed to give intervals
for quantities such as an asymptote. The uncertainty of the curve itself comes from
`ADREPORT()` on a grid of the predictor, as a pointwise confidence band calculated on an
unbounded scale.

A fitted model can be checked by simulating hypothetical samples from it and calculating
scaled quantile residuals, which are approximately uniform between 0 and 1 when the model
describes the data generating process. Their patterns show where the model disagrees with
the data, but not why. For the reed frogs they showed overdispersion relative to the
Binomial distribution, and a Beta-Binomial model with the same curve described the
variation among tanks. Candidate models fitted to the same observations are compared with
AIC, AICc and BIC, with the number of independent observations as $n$. The criteria rank
the candidates; what they mean for the question, and what remains uncertain, is a matter of
interpretation in ecological terms.

In this chapter every tank was an independent observation. In
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) the observations come in groups, such as repeated
measurements on the same individuals or sites, and the parameters of the curve vary among
groups.

# Chapter quiz

The questions below follow the order of the chapter. Try each question before opening its
solution.

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 1: hatching success and temperature"}

The number of eggs that hatch out of each clutch is described with a Binomial model, and a
Ricker curve of temperature, $aTe^{-bT}$, is proposed for the parameter of the distribution
that depends on temperature. Which parameter is that, and what can go wrong with this
curve? How could the curve be written so that it always has the right range?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The curve describes the probability that an egg hatches, which must lie between 0 and 1.
The Ricker curve has its maximum $a/(be)$ at $T=1/b$, and nothing stops this maximum from
exceeding 1 during the fit, in which case the Binomial probability is not defined. One
solution is to write the curve with its maximum as a parameter, $p(T)=h\,(T/c)\,e^{1-T/c}$,
whose peak has height $h$ at $T=c$, and to optimise $h$ on the logit scale so that it stays
between 0 and 1. Another is to pass a curve through the inverse logit.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 2: plant growth and soil nitrogen"}

A colleague describes the growth of plants against soil nitrogen with a hockey-stick curve,
which increases linearly up to a threshold $c$ and is flat above it. The NLL uses an `if`
that applies one formula or the other to each plant depending on whether its nitrogen is
below $c$, and the threshold is a parameter. What goes wrong when RTMB processes this NLL?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

RTMB records the calculations of the NLL at the starting values and differentiates them,
but a comparison between a parameter and a value has no derivative. By default RTMB refuses
it, so `MakeADFun()` stops with an error. If the comparison were recorded, only the side of
the `if` taken at the starting value of $c$ would be used, so during the fit every plant
would stay on that side, whatever value of $c$ the optimiser tried, and the estimate of the
threshold would be meaningless. Moreover, the curve has a sharp bend at $c$, where its
derivative does not exist. A smooth curve that approximates the bend avoids both problems.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 3: photosynthesis at low light"}

The rate of photosynthesis of leaves was measured at light intensities from 0 to
200 µmol/m²/s, where the response still increases almost linearly, and a Michaelis–Menten
curve was fitted. Which quantity of the curve do the data determine well, and which
parameters do they determine poorly? What would you expect of the correlation between the
estimates, and how would you improve the design?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The data cover only the initial rise of the curve, so they determine its initial slope,
$a/b$, well, but the asymptote $a$ and the half-saturation constant $b$ poorly: many
combinations with the same ratio give similar curves over the range of the data. The
estimates of $a$ and $b$ will therefore be strongly and positively correlated, and their
likelihood profile intervals wide and asymmetric. Measurements at higher light, where the
curve levels off, would determine the asymptote.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 4: a band for survival"}

The estimated probability that a seedling survives at a given soil moisture is 0.97, with a
standard error of 0.02 on the original scale. Calculate the Wald interval on the original
scale. Why do we calculate the confidence band of a probability on the logit scale?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

On the original scale the interval is $0.97\pm1.96\times0.02$, from 0.931 to 1.009, and its
upper endpoint is not a probability. On the logit scale the curve is unbounded, the Wald
interval cannot cross a bound, and the log-likelihood is usually closer to a parabola, so
the interval is more accurate. Its endpoints are transformed back with `plogis()`, which
keeps them between 0 and 1.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 5: fruits on shrubs"}

A report shows the expected number of fruits per shrub as a function of shrub height, with
a pointwise 95% confidence band. A reader expects about 95% of the shrubs to lie inside the
band. Is that right?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

No. The band describes the uncertainty of the curve, the expected number of fruits: at each
height, the interval contains the expected number under the data generating process at
that height in about 95% of hypothetical samples. The numbers of fruits of individual shrubs vary around the curve
according to the distribution of the observations, which is much wider than the band, so
many shrubs lie outside it.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 6: seedlings along a light gradient"}

The scaled quantile residuals of a Poisson model for the number of seedlings per quadrat,
with an exponential curve of light, are mostly below 0.5 at low light and mostly above 0.5
at high light. What does this mean? Does it tell you that the Poisson distribution is
wrong?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The observed counts are lower than the model predicts at low light and higher at high
light, so the curve misses a systematic change of the expected count with light: its shape
is wrong, or a predictor that changes with light is missing. The pattern does not say which,
and it says nothing in particular about the Poisson distribution. Revise the curve and check
the residuals again.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 7: germination in pots"}

A Binomial model is fitted to the number of seeds that germinate out of 25 in each pot, and
DHARMa gives a dispersion statistic of 0.45. What does this mean? Would a Beta-Binomial
model help?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The numbers germinated vary around the curve less than a Binomial model allows, about half
as much as a variance: this is underdispersion. It suggests that the seeds of a pot do not
behave as independent trials with the same probability (for example, because of
competition within the pot), although the residuals alone cannot say which assumption
fails. A Beta-Binomial model cannot help, because its variance is always at least that
of the Binomial model with the same mean.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 8: three models for germination"}

The germination of seeds in trays at five temperatures is described with three models: (a)
a Binomial model with a constant probability; (b) a Binomial model whose probability is the
inverse logit of $a+bT$; (c) a Beta-Binomial model with the same curve as (b). Which models
are nested in which, and how many parameters does each have?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

Model (a) is model (b) with $b=0$, so it is nested in (b). Model (b) is the limit of model
(c) as $\kappa$ grows without bound, so it is nested in (c). Model (a) is also nested in (c).
The models have one, two and three parameters: the probability; $a$ and $b$; and $a$, $b$
and $\kappa$.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 9: clutches of eggs"}

A Beta-Binomial model with three parameters is fitted to the number of hatched eggs in 30
clutches of 4 eggs each, and its maximum log-likelihood is $-41.2$. What is $n$ in BIC, and
what is the BIC of the model?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The independent observations are the clutches, because the eggs of a clutch share its
probability of hatching, so $n=30$ and not 120 eggs. Then
$\mathrm{BIC}=3\log(30)+2\times41.2\approx10.20+82.4=92.6$.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 10: seed removal by rodents"}

In each of 30 plots, 20 seeds are put out and the number removed by rodents after a week is
counted. Two Binomial models are fitted: (a) a constant probability of removal; (b) a
probability that decreases with the distance of the plot from shrub cover. The residuals of
model (b) show two plots that stand out, so a colleague removes them, fits model (b) again
to the other 28 plots, and finds that its AIC is lower than that of model (a), fitted to all
30 plots. What is wrong with this comparison, and what should be done instead?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The maximum log-likelihood is the log probability of the observations to which the model
was fitted, so the two AICs describe different data. The log probability of each plot is
negative, so every plot lowers the maximum log-likelihood: model (b) gains from having two
observations fewer, and more still because
the plots that it left out were the ones that it described worst. The difference in AIC
says nothing about which model is better. Every candidate must be fitted to the same plots:
all 30, or 28 for both models if there is a reason to exclude the two plots that does not
depend on the fit (such as a recording error). Plots that stand out in the residuals are
also information about the model, which may need another curve or a Beta-Binomial
distribution.

:::
::::
